t: Design SQL — Hash Maps per Table
o: A straightforward simulation/design problem. Each table needs: a column count for validation, an auto-increment id counter that survives deletions, storage mapping id -> row, and export in insertion-id order. Example 1 exercises insert/select/export/remove; note after removing id 1, selecting it returns "<null>" and exporting yields only id 2, while the next insert still gets id 3 (counter never resets). Invalid names, wrong row lengths, and missing cells must all be guarded.
k: Per-table state: {columns, nextId, Map<id,row>} covers all operations.
Auto-increment ids are never reused — keep nextId separate from stored rows.
Export must sort by id (or track insertion order) since removals create gaps.

a.i: Store tables in a hash map keyed by name. ins validates column count, assigns nextId++, stores the row. rmv deletes the key if present. sel checks table, row, and column bounds. exp joins id + cells with commas over sorted ids. All operations are O(1) except exp which is O(rows·cols).
s: ins: validate name and row length, store rows[nextId]=row, increment nextId.
rmv/sel: guard existence and bounds, then delete/read.
exp: iterate sorted ids building comma-joined strings.
a.t: O(1) per ins/rmv/sel; O(R log R + R·C) per exp due to sorting ids.

w: Follow-up answer: if tables become sparse from heavy deletion, replace the dense array with a hash map keyed by id (as done here) — memory becomes proportional to live rows rather than the highest id ever allocated, and operations stay O(1). Pitfalls: resetting nextId on delete, off-by-one on 1-indexed columnId, and forgetting null-table guards on every method.
